questions.question_prompt: What is the safety purpose of a correctly adjusted head restraint?
questions.keyed_answer: To reduce damaging head movement in a collision.
questions.teaching_excerpt: A correctly designed and adjusted head restraint helps limit damaging head movement relative to the torso and reduce neck-injury risk. Trafikverket advises positioning the top at the crown of the head and keeping the gap behind the head as small as possible. Adjust it for the occupant before driving; a comfort setting is not the same as a protective setting. A head restraint cannot guarantee that injury will be avoided. questions.question_prompt: Why does a car have separate brake circuits?
questions.keyed_answer: To retain some braking if one circuit fails.
questions.teaching_excerpt: Separate brake circuits provide a reserve: if one circuit fails, the remaining circuit can still provide some braking. This reduces the chance of losing all braking through one circuit fault. Remaining braking may be weaker; it is not permission to continue normally. The technical requirements distinguish the surviving capability from full service-brake performance. Transportstyrelsen: brake circuits ABS in an emergency. Anti-lock braking helps prevent wheel locking and can preserve steering control. questions.question_prompt: During an emergency stop, your ABS brake pedal pulsates. What should you normally do?
questions.keyed_answer: Maintain firm pressure and steer as needed.
questions.teaching_excerpt: keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer as necessary; do not pump the pedal. Pulsation or vibration through the pedal during ABS operation can be normal feedback as the system regulates braking. This differs from a changed pedal feel in ordinary braking. ABS does not guarantee a shorter stop or create grip that the tyres lack. UK Government: ABS instruction, Rule 120 · Ford: normal ABS feedback, 2011 Explorer Recognise a symptom, then act. questions.question_prompt: Why are parts of a car designed to deform in a crash?
questions.keyed_answer: To absorb energy and reduce the forces reaching occupants.
questions.teaching_excerpt: Crumple zones are parts of a vehicle designed to deform progressively in a collision, absorbing energy while the passenger compartment's structure protects the occupants' space. Spreading the deceleration over a longer time reduces forces acting on the people inside. A car remaining visually undamaged is not the objective: designed deformation can be part of its protection. Belts and suitable child restraints still matter, and no structure makes every collision survivable. Western Australia government: structure and crumple zones Practice example.
